sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

content.text: For this isolated validation, my established standing preference is UTC timestamps in status reports. Hold this preference in conversation for the next automatic stow; do not write any files yet. Reply with 1200 words about time zones, then finish with READY_INITIAL.

Time zones are one of the most consequential invisible systems in modern life. They structure how people schedule work, when markets open, how airplanes are coordinated, when laws take effect, and how software stores and displays the moment something happened. At a glance a time zone is only an offset from Coordinated Universal Time, yet behind that offset sits a long history of astronomy, politics, railroads, empires, labor movements, and computing conventions. Understanding time zones is therefore not only a matter of knowing that New York is often UTC−5 or that Tokyo is UTC+9; it is a matter of understanding why civil time is regional, why it changes, and why machines and humans keep disagreeing about “now.”

Before standardized zones, most towns kept solar time. Noon was when the sun crossed the local meridian. That arrangement was natural for agricultural life and short travel, but it became intolerable once railways and telegraphs connected distant cities. A train timetable written in dozens of slightly different local noons was a recipe for missed connections and accidents. In the nineteenth century, railway companies and governments pushed toward broader standard times. Britain’s railways popularized Greenwich mean time; in North America, continental zones were proposed and adopted in stages; other regions followed with their own schemes. The result was not a pure scientific partition of the globe into twenty-four equal slices. It was a patchwork shaped by borders, trade routes, and political identity. Some countries span many longitudes yet keep a single national time to reinforce unity. Others split into several zones. A few places offset by thirty or forty-five minutes rather than whole hours, preserving local compromise.

Coordinated Universal Time, UTC, became the reference backbone. UTC is not exactly the old Greenwich mean time, and it is not pure atomic time either; it is atomic time steered by occasional leap seconds so that it stays close to Earth’s rotation. For most civil and business purposes, people do not live in UTC. They live in named zones that map a region to an offset and to a rule set about daylight saving. The IANA time zone database, often called the tz database or zoneinfo, is the practical encyclopedia of those rules. It records not only present offsets but historical changes: when a government shifted a boundary, abolished daylight saving, or moved the clocks by an unusual amount. Software that wants correct local time for a civil date in the past must consult that history. A timestamp labeled only with a fixed offset is incomplete if you later need to know what wall clocks in a city showed on a given calendar day years ago.

Daylight saving time complicates everything. The idea is simple—shift clocks to make evening daylight last longer in summer—but the implementation is political and irregular. Jurisdictions adopt it, repeal it, change transition dates, or apply it unevenly. Transition days create repeated or missing local hours. Ambiguous times occur when clocks fall back; nonexistent times occur when they spring forward. APIs that convert between “local civil time” and instant timestamps must define policies for those gaps. Users who schedule a meeting for 1:30 a.m. on a fall-back night may not realize that 1:30 a.m. happens twice. Distributed systems that naively store local times without zone identifiers accumulate silent errors that surface years later in audits, billing, or legal discovery.

In computing, the safest internal representation for an instant is usually a UTC-based timestamp or a monotonic count from an epoch, with zone and calendar information applied at the edges for display and input. That pattern separates “when it happened in physics-like time” from “how people in a place name that moment.” RFC 3339 and ISO 8601 strings with explicit offsets are far clearer than bare clock readings. Still, offsets alone do not capture future daylight-saving rule changes; a zone name such as America/New_York carries rule logic that a static −05:00 does not. Calendars, reminders, and airline systems therefore often store both an instant and a zone or a civil local time plus zone, depending on whether the intent is a fixed instant or a civil wall time that should float with political rules.

Globalization makes these distinctions daily practical problems. A team spread across San Francisco, London, Nairobi, and Singapore has overlapping work windows that shrink to a few hours. Status reports, incident timelines, and release notes benefit from a single reference zone so that readers do not mentally juggle conversions. UTC is a common choice for engineering status because it is seasonless in the daylight-saving sense and widely understood in technical communities. That does not mean UTC is “more true” for human life; it means it is a stable lingua franca for ordering events. Product interfaces still ought to show local times for end users, with UTC available for support and operations. Mixed audiences need clear labeling: “14:00 UTC (09:00 America/New_York).” Ambiguity is the enemy.

Aviation, shipping, and the internet’s core protocols lean heavily on UTC. Flight plans, NOTAMs, and many log formats assume it. Financial markets, by contrast, still speak in venue-local times: an exchange opens at a civil clock time in its city, and regulations may be written that way. Cryptographic systems timestamp in UTC or Unix time to avoid locality. Collaboration software must bridge these cultures. When an outage timeline is written, investigators reconstructing causality want a monotonic ordering; when executives read a summary, they may prefer their headquarters zone. Good reporting practice states the zone once and sticks to it, or always includes the zone beside every time.

Astronomy and space operations add another layer. Telescope schedules depend on sidereal time and Earth orientation; spacecraft use mission elapsed time and onboard clocks synchronized under relativistic constraints. Even there, ground teams convert back to UTC for coordination. GPS time and other GNSS time scales differ from UTC by known offsets and leap-second handling; converters must be explicit. The deeper lesson is that “time” is plural: Earth rotation, atomic resonance, civil policy, and mission counters are related but not identical.

Human factors remain stubborn. People forget offsets when traveling. Phone auto-zone updates can shift calendar notifications unexpectedly. Recurring meetings encoded in local time may jump when DST starts; recurring meetings encoded as UTC instants stay fixed on the timeline but drift relative to local workdays. Neither choice is universally correct; the right representation depends on whether the series is “every Monday at 10:00 in Berlin” or “every seven times twenty-four hours from this instant.” Designers should ask what the user meant, not only what the database column type allows.

Legal systems care about time zones more than casual users expect. Contracts specify governing law and sometimes define when a notice is deemed received—end of a business day in a particular city, or midnight UTC. Courts have litigated disputes over filing deadlines at zone boundaries. Regulatory disclosures and securities rules can hinge on the clock at a specific exchange. Forensics and compliance logs must preserve trustworthy timestamps; clock skew between machines then becomes an evidentiary problem. Network time protocol, secure time sources, and auditable synchronization are part of security posture, not mere convenience.

The politics of zones still evolve. Countries occasionally announce sudden offset changes for energy policy, election symbolism, or alignment with trading partners. Islands and border towns may follow a neighboring country’s time for economic reasons despite belonging to another sovereign. Maps that color the world into neat bands hide these exceptions. Data maintainers at IANA and in operating-system vendors track bulletins and push updates; devices that do not update zone data mis-convert future local times. Embedded systems and air-gapped machines are especially vulnerable to stale rules.

Teaching time zones well means teaching both mechanism and humility. Mechanism includes offsets, abbreviations (which are ambiguous: CST can mean several things), DST transitions, Unix epochs, leap seconds, and the difference between instant and civil time. Humility includes expecting missing context in human messages like “tomorrow at 5,” expecting bugs at transition weekends, and expecting that a “simple” display change can corrupt historical interpretation if zone identity is stripped. Writers of status reports can reduce friction by choosing one reference convention and labeling it. In technical settings, UTC timestamps are a strong default precisely because they minimize seasonal and national special cases in the narrative of events, while still allowing readers to convert to local zones when they care about lived experience.

Looking forward, debates continue about abolishing daylight saving, adopting permanent standard or permanent daylight time, and simplifying offsets. Leap seconds are being reconsidered because smearing or discontinuities hurt computer systems. As more work becomes asynchronous and globally distributed, the cultural weight of a single shared “business day” lessens, and precise universal timestamps gain importance. Yet people will still wake with the sun. Civil time will remain a negotiated interface between planetary rotation, atomic measurement, and community preference. Software and organizations that treat that interface carefully—storing instants cleanly, preserving zone context, updating rule databases, and communicating times with explicit labels—will avoid whole classes of confusion that have nothing to do with the underlying product and everything to do with the clock.

In daily operational practice, conventions matter as much as theory. A team that quietly agrees that status reports, incident timelines, deployment markers, and cross-region check-ins are always written in UTC builds a shared index of events. Readers learn to scan a document without reinterpreting each line. Local times can still appear in parentheses when an event is inherently local, such as a store opening or a regional broadcast. The point is not to erase geography; it is to prevent geography from scrambling the order and meaning of reported facts. Clear conventions also help newcomers. Instead of inferring house style from scattered examples, they see a stable pattern. Over time that pattern becomes part of institutional memory, reducing the small transactional tax paid every time someone asks “wait, is that your time or my time?”

Time zones, then, are infrastructure for trust in shared schedules. They encode history and power, but they also offer tools—UTC especially—for coordinating without constant renegotiation. Using them consciously is a small discipline with outsized returns in clarity.

READY_INITIAL
